concept.technique_name: Nikhilam complement method for decimal conversion

solution.description: Write 17 over 76 as a division to be carried out, fixing 17 as the numerator and 76 as the divisor before any digits are produced.

solution.operation: Apply Nikhilam Sutra (All from 9, last from 10) to denominator
solution.description: Raise 76 to the next power of ten, 100, and take all from 9 and the last from 10 to get the complement 24, the amount by which 76 falls short of 100.

solution.operation: Set up the division using the complement
solution.description: Rewrite the denominator as 100 minus that complement, so the division can be steered by the small number 24 rather than by 76 head on.

solution.operation: Perform division using the complement method
solution.description: Work the division with the complement in hand, releasing one decimal digit at a time, which gives 0.22368421 out to the eight places asked for.
Check the work by multiplying the eight-place decimal back by 76; it returns 17 to the accuracy kept, so the digits stand.

examples.problem_statement: Using the Vedic mathematics technique of osculation, determine if 21 is divisible by 7. The Ekādhika (Positive Osculator) for 7 is 5. The process involves multiplying the last digit by the Ekādhika and adding it to the previous digits. If the result is the divisor itself (7) or a repetition of a previous result, then the number is divisible by 7.

solution.description: For divisor 7, the Ekādhika is calculated as (7 × 1 + 1)/2 = 4, but the standard Ekādhika for 7 is 5. This is a known value in Vedic Mathematics.
We begin with the number we want to test for divisibility by 7

solution.operation: Take the last digit (1) and multiply by Ekādhika (5)
solution.description: The osculation process requires multiplying the last digit by the Ekādhika

solution.operation: Add the result to the remaining digits (2)
solution.description: The product is added to the remaining digits to get the next number in the sequence
Since we reached the divisor (7) itself, the original number is divisible by 7
Osculate 237 by 8: Multiply last digit 7 by 8, add previous digit 3 to get 59, then multiply 9 by 8 and add 2 to get 74, showing multi-digit osculation.
Osculate 4321 by 7: Start from right, multiply 1 by 7, add 2 to get 9; multiply 9 by 7, add 3 to get 66; multiply 6 by 7, add 4 to get 46, illustrating full number osculation.

key_reminders: {'point': ':—We need not carry this process indefinitely on.'}
{'point': 'Hence the importance of the Ekādhika.'}

examples.problem_statement: Test whether 2774 is divisible by 19 using osculation with Ekādhika 2.

solution.description: Because 19 ends in 9, add 1 and divide by 10 to get the Ekadhika 2; this one multiplier drives every step that follows.

solution.operation: Start with the rightmost digit (4) and multiply by Ekādhika (2)
solution.description: Take the rightmost digit of 2774, which is 4, and multiply it by the Ekadhika 2 to get 8, the first osculation product.

solution.operation: Add the product to the next digit (7) on the left
solution.description: Add that 8 to the next digit leftward, 7, giving 15; 15 is now the running total that will itself be osculated.

solution.operation: Multiply the result (15) by Ekādhika (2) and add to the next digit (7)
solution.description: Osculate the running total rather than a single digit: 15 times 2 is 30, and adding the next digit leftward, 7, gives 37.

solution.operation: Multiply the result (37) by Ekādhika (2) and add to the next digit (2)
solution.description: Do it once more against the leading digit: 37 times 2 is 74, and adding the leftmost 2 gives 76, the final osculation total.
Test that total: 76 divided by 19 is 4 with nothing left over, so the original number 2774 is divisible by 19.

examples.answer: The final remainder is 0, indicating 2774 is divisible by 19

key_reminders: {'point': 'Note that the osculation of any number by its own Ekādhika will go on giving that very number or a multiple thereof.'}
common_mistakes: Starting the osculation at the leftmost digit 2 instead of at the rightmost digit 4
Multiplying only the newest digit by 2 instead of multiplying the whole running total before adding the next digit
Reading the Ekadhika for 19 off the digits 1 and 9; it comes from (19 + 1) divided by 10, which is 2

examples.problem_statement: Determine whether 5293240096 is divisible by 139 (or not)

solution.operation: Apply current (long division) method: divide 5293240096 by 139.
solution.description: Start with the familiar route and divide 5293240096 by 139 in full long division, so there is a benchmark the Vedic method must reproduce.

solution.operation: Observe remainder is 0 after full division.
solution.result: Ekādhika = (divisor * n + 1)/10 where n is chosen so that product ends in 9
solution.description: The long division ends with nothing left over, so 139 goes into 5293240096 exactly; that is the fact the osculation has to recover.

solution.operation: Apply Vedic method using Ekādhika (osculator) = 14 for divisor 139.
solution.result: Ekādhika = (divisor * n + 1)/10 where n is chosen so that product ends in 9
solution.description: Now take the Vedic route: since 139 ends in 9, add 1 and divide by 10 to get the osculator 14, the only multiplier the method needs.
Osculate along the number: strip the last digit, multiply it by 14, add it back to the digits that remain, and repeat across the row.
The successive totals fall from 529324093 through 5293259, 52959 and 556 down to 139 itself; landing on the divisor settles divisibility without finishing a long division.

concept.technique_name: Ekādhika (Positive Osculator) method for divisibility by numbers ending in 9

examples.problem_statement: Determine whether $5293240096$ is divisible by $139$ using both conventional long division and the Vedic method with Ekādhika (osculator).

solution.operation: Find the Ekādhika (osculator) for divisor 139: Since 139 ends in 9, multiply the last digit by 1 and add 1 to get the osculator: $139 \rightarrow 13 \times 1 + 1 = 14$.
Remove the last digit (6), multiply it by 14: $6 \times 14 = 84$, add to the rest: $529324009 + 84 = 529324093$.
Repeat: remove last digit (3), multiply by 14: $3 \times 14 = 42$, add: $52932409 + 42 = 52932451$.
Since the result is 139 (the divisor), the original number is divisible by 139.
Since we reach 139 (the divisor), the number is divisible by 139
By the current method (long division): $5293240096 \div 139 = 380864$ with a remainder of $0$, so it is divisible.
By the Vedic method: For the divisor $139$, the Ekādhika (osculator) is $14$.
Apply osculation to $5293240096$ using the osculator $14$.
Since the final osculation result $139$ is divisible by $139$, the original number $5293240096$ is also divisible by $139$.

examples.problem_statement: Using the negative osculation method, determine if 165763 is divisible by 41. The negative osculator for 41 is 4. Also, verify using the osculation results: 16564, 1640, 164, and 0.

solution.result: For divisor 41, negative osculator = 4 (since 4 × 1 = 4, and 4 + 1 = 5, which is a multiple of 5, but the rule is: for numbers ending in 1, the negative osculator is the number formed by all digits except the last)
solution.description: For a divisor ending in 1, the negative osculator is what is left when that final 1 is dropped, so 41 gives 4; every step below multiplies by 4 and subtracts.

solution.operation: Start with 165763. Remove last digit (3), multiply by osculator (4), subtract from remaining number
solution.description: Peel the last digit 3 off 165763, multiply it by the osculator 4 to get 12, and take that from the remaining 16576, leaving 16564.

solution.operation: Take 16564. Remove last digit (4), multiply by 4, subtract from remaining number
solution.description: Repeat on 16564: its last digit 4 times 4 is 16, subtracted from the remaining 1656 to give 1640.

solution.operation: Take 1640. Remove last digit (0), multiply by 4, subtract from remaining number
solution.description: Repeat on 1640: the last digit is 0, so nothing is subtracted and 164 carries forward unchanged, though the digit is still consumed.

solution.operation: Take 164. Remove last digit (4), multiply by 4, subtract from remaining number
solution.description: Repeat on 164: its last digit 4 times 4 is 16, and 16 minus 16 leaves 0.
A final value of 0 counts as a multiple of 41, so the chain shows 165763 is divisible by 41.
Settle the negative osculator for 71 before touching the number: dropping the final 1 leaves 7, so each pass will multiply the last digit by 7 and subtract.
Apply that rule repeatedly, each pass replacing the number by its leading digits minus 7 times its last digit, until what remains is small enough to recognise as a multiple of 71 or not.

Stopping as soon as the running value looks small; only 0 or a genuine multiple of the divisor settles the question
Skipping the digit 0 in 1640 because it subtracts nothing, when it still has to be consumed as a step
